raw_text:
### Introduction
Atrial fibrillation (AF) is a major global health challenge, significantly increasing the risk of thromboembolic stroke [15,16,27]. In nonvalvular AF, more than 90% of stroke-inducing thrombi originate within the left atrial appendage (LAA) [1]. While oral anticoagulants (OACs)—including vitamin K antagonists (VKAs) and direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs)—are the first-line therapy for stroke prevention, their long-term use is often limited by major bleeding, poor adherence, or absolute contraindications [15,16]. Consequently, percutaneous left atrial appendage closure (LAAC) has emerged as a crucial mechanical, non-pharmacological alternative for stroke prophylaxis [11,12]. This review synthesizes the clinical evidence, device technologies, procedural imaging, post-implant pharmacotherapy, and future outlook of percutaneous LAAC.

### Clinical Evidence and Evolution of Devices
The efficacy of percutaneous LAAC was established by the landmark PROTECT AF [2] and PREVAIL [3] randomized controlled trials (RCTs), comparing the first-generation Watchman 2.5 device (Boston Scientific) with warfarin. Long-term 5-year follow-up demonstrated that LAAC provided comparable protection against ischemic stroke and systemic embolism, with a significant reduction in hemorrhagic stroke, disabling/fatal stroke, and cardiovascular mortality compared to warfarin [4]. For patients with absolute contraindications to OAC, the ASAP study demonstrated the feasibility of LAAC followed only by dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) [22]. Large registries, such as EWOLUTION [13,23] and the Global Amulet Registry [14], confirmed high procedural success (>95%) and safety in routine practice.

As clinical practice transitioned to DOACs, the PRAGUE-17 trial directly compared LAAC (using Watchman or Amplatzer Amulet devices) with DOACs in high-risk patients [5]. The 4-year outcomes confirmed that LAAC is noninferior to DOACs in preventing major cardiovascular, neurological, or bleeding events [6].

Device iterations have substantially improved procedural safety. The next-generation Watchman FLX device, featuring a fully enclosed distal end and more anchors, showed a remarkably low periprocedural safety event rate of 0.5% in the PINNACLE FLX trial [8], with favorable outcomes sustained at 2 years [30]. Concurrently, the Amplatzer Amulet (Abbott) employs a dual-seal (lobe and disc) mechanism to cover the LAA ostium. The Amulet IDE trial demonstrated that the Amulet was noninferior to the first-generation Watchman for stroke prevention and superior in achieving complete LAA occlusion [7], with clinical outcomes remaining comparable out to 5 years [29]. The SWISS-APERO trial, a head-to-head comparison of the Watchman FLX and Amulet, confirmed high procedural success for both, highlighting slight differences in sealing performance and residual leak patterns [9]. For complex LAA anatomies, specialized devices like the self-expanding LAmbre system also show excellent performance [24]. The concept of LAA closure received further validation from the surgical LAAOS III trial, which showed a 33% reduction in stroke when the LAA was occluded during concomitant cardiac surgery [10].

### Procedural Technique and Imaging
Accurate pre-procedural planning and intraprocedural imaging are paramount. Multi-detector computed tomography (CT) angiography has emerged as a gold standard for 3D anatomical reconstruction, allowing precise sizing and device selection [12]. While transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) remains the traditional gold standard for intraprocedural guidance, intracardiac echocardiography (ICE) has emerged as a highly effective alternative, allowing the procedure to be performed under conscious sedation without general anesthesia, as outlined in recent expert consensus documents [28]. Large-scale real-world data from the National Cardiovascular Data Registry (NCDR) LAAO Registry have confirmed high procedural success rates and low complication rates in everyday clinical practice [26].

### Complications and Post-procedural Management
Post-procedural pharmacology is critical to prevent device-related thrombus (DRT) before complete endothelization occurs (typically within 45 days). While the classic Watchman regimen involved 45 days of warfarin/aspirin followed by DAPT [2,3], modern clinical practice increasingly utilizes DOAC-based regimens [11]. In patients at high risk of bleeding, half-dose DOAC regimens have been shown to significantly reduce bleeding while maintaining low rates of DRT [20]. 

Despite high success rates, late complications such as DRT [17,19] and peridevice leak (PDL) [18,25] remain challenges. DRT, which occurs in 1% to 4% of cases, is associated with a significantly increased risk of ischemic stroke and requires prompt treatment with anticoagulation [17]. Furthermore, insights from the NCDR LAAO Registry indicate that even small (1–5 mm) residual PDLs are associated with a modest but statistically significant increase in thromboembolic events [18].

### Future Directions and Guidelines
Current ESC [15,27] and ACC/AHA [16] guidelines recommend percutaneous LAAC (Class IIb) for stroke prevention in patients with nonvalvular AF who have a clear contraindication to long-term oral anticoagulation. However, the landscape is shifting. The OPTION trial recently demonstrated that in patients undergoing catheter ablation for AF, LAAC is noninferior to DOACs for thromboembolic protection while offering superior bleeding outcomes at 36 months [21]. Ongoing large-scale randomized trials will further clarify whether percutaneous LAAC can serve as a first-line alternative to DOAC therapy in a broader AF population.

### Conclusion
Percutaneous left atrial appendage closure is a safe and effective therapeutic strategy for stroke prevention in patients with atrial fibrillation. Driven by iterative device designs, improved multi-modality imaging, and optimized post-procedural pharmacotherapy, LAAC has cemented its role as a viable alternative to oral anticoagulation, with its indications poised to expand further.
